title: Given an array of positive integers and a target value, find the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to the target, returning zero if no such subarray exists. Solve it with the sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Minimum Size Subarray Sum (Shortest Subarray with Sum At Least Target)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for the smallest length of a contiguous subarray whose elements sum to at least a given target, assuming all elements are positive. It is solved with a variable-size sliding window: a right pointer adds elements to a running sum until the sum reaches the target, then a left pointer shrinks the window as far as possible while the sum stays at or above the target, recording the smallest window length each time the condition holds. It runs in linear time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a sequence of daily deposit amounts into Priya's current account and wants to know the fewest consecutive days needed to accumulate at least a target amount, say two hundred thousand rupees, for a liquidity certificate. He slides a window: he keeps adding days on the right until he reaches the target, then trims days off the left as long as he still meets the target, always remembering the shortest qualifying span.
s1_definition.oneliner: Grow right until the sum reaches the target, then shrink left while it still qualifies, tracking the shortest window.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for the smallest length of a contiguous subarray whose elements sum to at least a given target, assuming all elements are positive. It is solved with a variable-size sliding window: a right pointer adds elements to a running sum until the sum reaches the target, then a left pointer shrinks the window as far as possible while the sum stays at or above the target, recording the smallest window length each time the condition holds. It runs in linear time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a sequence of daily deposit amounts into Priya's current account and wants to know the fewest consecutive days needed to accumulate at least a target amount, say two hundred thousand rupees, for a liquidity certificate. He slides a window: he keeps adding days on the right until he reaches the target, then trims days off the left as long as he still meets the target, always remembering the shortest qualifying span.

**One line to remember:** Grow right until the sum reaches the target, then shrink left while it still qualifies, tracking the shortest window.

sections.s2_technical:
We maintain a window with a left and a right boundary and a running sum of the elements currently inside it. The right pointer moves forward across the array, and each time it includes a new element we add that element to the running sum with `sum += nums[right]`. This expansion phase continues naturally as the loop advances.

The important phase is the shrink. After adding each element, we check whether the running sum is at least the target. While it is, the current window qualifies, so we record its length with `best = Math.min(best, right - left + 1)` and then try to make it smaller: we subtract the leftmost element with `sum -= nums[left]` and advance the left pointer. We keep shrinking inside a `while (sum >= target)` loop, because removing one element might still leave the sum above the target, and we want the smallest possible window ending at the current right position.

The reason this is correct and linear rests entirely on all elements being positive. Because every element is positive, adding elements strictly increases the sum and removing elements strictly decreases it, so the sum behaves monotonically as the window grows or shrinks. That monotonic behaviour is what lets us greedily shrink from the left without missing a shorter answer. The senior-level nuance is that if the array could contain negatives or zeros, this simple window breaks and we would need a prefix-sum plus a monotonic deque instead, which is a genuinely different and harder algorithm.

We initialize the best length to a sentinel such as `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, and at the end if it was never updated we return zero to signal that no qualifying subarray exists. The time complexity is linear, O(n), since the right pointer advances n times and the left pointer only moves forward, so the combined movement is at most 2n. The space complexity is O(1), just a running sum and a few indices.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the treasury desk reviews a sequence of daily net deposit inflows into a corporate current account and must certify the shortest number of consecutive days during which the account accumulated at least a required liquidity threshold. Regulators want to see that the account can reach the threshold quickly, and a shorter qualifying span is stronger evidence of healthy cash flow. This is exactly the minimum-size-subarray-sum problem, where each day's inflow is a positive amount and the threshold is the target.

Problem 2 — Testing every possible span of days by brute force is quadratic and will not scale across the bank's large base of corporate accounts and long reporting histories. The linear sliding window, which relies on inflows being positive, gives one pass per account, which is what makes the certification batch finish on time.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `LiquidityCertifier` service with a `shortestDaysToReach` method implementing the window using int amounts for clarity in the DSA demo while noting production would use BigDecimal, and a runnable `MinSubarraySumDemo` main class that certifies Rajesh's and Priya's inflow sequences against a target, logging each shrink at fine level and the final answer at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's inflows are 50000, 30000, 80000, 40000, 100000 with target 200000. We keep a left boundary at 0, a running sum of 0, and a best of a large sentinel value.

Step 1: Right at index 0, add 50000, sum is 50000, below target, no shrink.

Step 2: Right at index 1, add 30000, sum is 80000, below target, no shrink.

Step 3: Right at index 2, add 80000, sum is 160000, below target, no shrink.

Step 4: Right at index 3, add 40000, sum is 200000, which meets the target. Record window length 4 (indices 0 to 3), best becomes 4. Shrink: subtract 50000 at left 0, sum is 150000, left moves to 1. Now below target, stop shrinking.

Step 5: Right at index 4, add 100000, sum is 250000, which meets the target. Record window length 4 (indices 1 to 4), best stays 4. Shrink: subtract 30000 at left 1, sum is 220000, still meets target, record window length 3 (indices 2 to 4), best becomes 3, left moves to 2. Subtract 80000 at left 2, sum is 140000, below target, stop.

No more elements. The best qualifying span is 3 days, the window of 80000, 40000, 100000 summing to 220000.

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum reaches at least a target, where all elements are positive, and I solve it with a variable-size sliding window in linear time. I keep a left boundary, a right pointer, and a running sum. The right pointer advances and adds each new element to the sum. Whenever the sum reaches the target the current window qualifies, so I record its length and then greedily shrink from the left, subtracting elements and advancing the left boundary while the sum stays at or above the target, which finds the shortest qualifying window ending at the current position. I start the best length at a sentinel and return zero if no window ever qualifies.

The point I always emphasize is that the correctness of the greedy shrink depends entirely on all elements being positive. Because positivity makes the sum increase as the window grows and decrease as it shrinks, the sum moves monotonically, which is exactly what lets me shrink aggressively without risking a missed shorter answer. If the array could contain negative numbers, this window would break, and I would instead need a prefix-sum array combined with a monotonic deque, which is a meaningfully harder algorithm.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the treasury desk. We reviewed a sequence of daily net inflows into a corporate current account and had to certify the shortest run of consecutive days during which the account accumulated at least a regulatory liquidity threshold, because a shorter qualifying span is stronger evidence of healthy cash flow. Each inflow was a positive amount, so the greedy window applied directly, and the linear pass let the certification batch scale across the bank's large base of corporate accounts.

The senior-level point I make is that this is the shrink-aggressively variant of the sliding window, the mirror image of problems where we grow aggressively, and knowing which direction to be greedy in is the real skill. I also call out that in production I would use BigDecimal for the money and guard against overflow by accumulating in a long, and that the moment negatives enter the data I must switch algorithms. Flagging that boundary between the easy positive case and the hard general case is what signals real depth to an interviewer.
